My questions are related the bolded sentence "A certified translator will provide both a certified translation and certified copies of the original documents.". Could you please answer the following questions:

3) Since a certified translator is allowed by IRCC to provide a certified copy of the original document, should "a certified translator" or " a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada" be added to the list of persons "who can certify copies" in the Guides to be consistent?

threads.answer:
Good afternoon Thank you for submitting your query to the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please accept our apologies for the late response. Please find the responses to your questions below.
1) A certified translator refers to a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada, am I right? Yes, your interpretation here is correct.
2) A certified translation done by a certified translator who also provides a certified copy of the original document does not need a separate "certified true copy" of the original document done by a notary public any more, am I right? Yes, your interpretation is correct here also. For any document not in English or French, if it is translated by a certified translator, then they will also be able to produce a "certified copy” of the original document. In this case, the applicant would no longer be required to get a "certified copy" of the document from one of the 3 options listed in the guide.
3) Since a certified translator is allowed by IRCC to provide a certified copy of the original document, should "a certified translator" or " a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada" be added to the list of persons "who can certify copies" in the Guides to be consistent? The reason "certified translators" are not listed in the guide of "who can certify copies?" is because IRCC does not want to direct people to “certified translators" just for the purpose of having a "certified copy” of a document created. However, if they need a document translated in the first place, they can have it translated and create a "certified copy" in the same place from the same person without having to go to a notary public, commissioner of oaths, or commissioner of taking affidavits. The only time they would need to have a translation and "certified copy" generated in two different places is if the translator IS NOT a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada. In this case, the translator would do the translation, but they would need to have a "certified copy" made elsewhere from one of the 3 options listed in the guide. In other words, "certified translators" can create "certified copies" of the document they are translating, but cannot be used to certify copies of other documents which is why they are not included on the list of persons "who can certify copies." We hope this addresses your concerns. Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. 1. 1. If an international student applies for a study permit extension to change their DLl, and their application is refused, while their original study permit for their initial DLI remains valid, is their original study permit still considered valid? Can the student continue studying at their original DLI without interruption? Response: When a student applies to extend their current study permit because they wish to change DLls, they must continue to be enrolled and study at their current DLl while their new application is being processed. It is only when their new study permit application is approved that the student is able to study at the new DLl. Therefore, if the application is refused there is no impact as the student was already studying at their initial DLl.
2. 2. If a student intends to take specific courses at another DLl temporarily, with the aim of transferring credits back to their original DLl, and accordingly applies for a new study permit for this secondary institution, can the student concurrently study at their originai DLi under their existing valid study permit? Response: A student can study at multiple DLls and hold a study permit for each DLI. Additional information is available by consulting the IRCC website.
3. 3. Can a study permit be linked to only one DLI at a time? In cases where a student holds two valid study permits due to the new DLI change policy, how does IRCC determine which institution the student's study permit is officially linked to? Response: While students may hold two valid study permits, students still need to ensure that they meet both study permit conditions and are actively studying as DLIs must provide enrollment status information to IRCC through the compliance reporting. Also, it is to be noted that it may be difficult for a student to be studying full- time at 2 DLls. When IRCC receives a study permit application, it is thoroughly assessed and reviewed by an officer before a decision is made.
Thank you kindly,

Hello,
This is in response to your follow up request of May 29th regarding eligibility of students to work from the time that they've graduated from one program of study until they start their subsequent program of study.
The guidance you've received from the Immigration Representatives mailbox in June 2015 with regards to student's ability to work from the time that they've graduated from one program of study until they start their subsequent program of study is no longer valid. As per R186(v)(i), a foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit if they are a holder of a study permit and they are full time student enrolled at a designated learning institution. As upon reception of their graduation letter, they are no longer considered a full-time student enrolled in a DLl, they cannot pursue working without a permit anymore. Therefore, we suggest that you advise students who've graduated from one program and are awaiting to start their next program in the fall to cease work off campus as soon as they receive the letter of graduation from their current designated learning institution, as they are no longer considered a full-time student and do not meet the eligibility requirements to work off campus.They will be able to reinitiate to work off campus upon the start of their program of study in the fall, if they meet the eligibility requirements for work off campus.
Furthermore, please note that we are currently working on the update to the Off-Campus Work PDl to add more clarification to the requirements.
Please note that if the student decided to apply for a PGWP after graduation, the student must cease work off campus between the time they've received their letter of graduation and the day that they apply for a post-graduation work permit program. Once the student applies for a post-graduation work permit, the transition period to a post-graduate work permit begins and they may work full time awaiting for a decision on their PGWP application. Applicants must cease working if their work permit application under the PGWPP is refused.

You have submitted two inquiries with similar questions. One in December 2016 below, and one in February 2017. reference number REP-2017-0283. It was responded to with the following information, which answers both inquiries:
What is the procedure, for a permanent resident of Canada who won their appeal at IAD on Residency Obligation (for a PR applied for PRTD and was found by the Visa office not to have met the Residency obligation, but the decision of officer was set aside by the lAD).
Will the Visa office continue to process the PRTD? In a situation where the Immigration Appeal Division (lAD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) allows an appeal of a negative residency determination decision made outside of Canada, the lAD sets aside the original decision and as per subsection 67(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and will "substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, including the making of a removal order, or refer the matter to the appropriate decision-maker for reconsideration." Where an appeal of a negative residency determination is allowed, the CBSA will inform IRCC of the IAD decision so that IRCC may take the necessary steps which will depend on the specific decision made by the lAD. The client would not need to make a new PRTD application as the original application would continue to be processed. The client may, however, wish to provide the notice they received from the lAD that the appeal was allowed to the processing office. Contact information for IRCC can be found on the IRCC website at [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/offices/index.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/offices/index.asp).
How long after the IAD decision will they process the PRTD? Is there a time limit before the visa office must process the PRTD? What is the procedure or recourse does the PR have, if the Visa office does not continue to process the PRTD in the specified time period? There is no specific timeframe for the office to complete the processing of the PRTD application following the lAD's decision; however, as soon as IRCC receives notification of the lAD decision, they will process the request as quickly as possible. Should the client wish to do so, they may also provide the notice they received from the lAD that the appeal was allowed to the processing office. If the application is taking longer than expected or the client needs to contact IRCC for any other reason regarding their PRTD application, they may contact the office processing their application. Contact information for IRCC can be found on the IRCC website at [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/offices/index.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/offices/index.asp).

threads.answer:
Dear Mrs
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Per our application guides, any document that is not in English or French must be accompanied by all three of the following:
the English or French translation; and an affidavit from the person who completed the translation; and a certified copy of the original document.
Translations may be done by a person who is fluent in both languages (English or French and the unofficial language). The translation must be accompanied by an affidavit swearing to the accuracy of the translation and the language proficiency of the translator.
An affidavit for a translation is a document stating that the translation is a true and accurate version of the original text. The translator swears in front of a commissioner authorized to administer oaths in the country where the translator lives, that the contents of their translation are a true translation and representation of the contents of the original document.
In regards to your questions, any Notary Public or Commissioner of Oaths independent of the translation service can certify the translation. Also, the certification needs to appear on a copy of the original document, in form of a stamp, and not on the original document itself.
We trust this information will assist you.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question: Can the employer simply agree to reduce the employee's hours without first filing a new Offer of Employment for an LMIA exempt work permit through the Employer Portal?
Response: Under the International Mobility Program employer compliance regime, the employer is required to provide the temporary worker with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same or better than those indicated in the offer of employment. Working conditions include non-wage related remuneration benefits and entitlements such as hours of work.
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not.
In order to reduce the hours of work for a temporary worker – and remain compliant with regulatory conditions-the employer can submit a new offer of employment as well as pay the $230 compliance fee. The worker must then apply for a new work permit using the new offer of employment number.
Alternatively, since foreign workers generally only are required to obtain a new work permit when either the employer or job or location changes, proactive notification to IRCC of salary and hours of work changes is not required under the International Mobility Program. The employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that worker is getting what was stated in the initial offer submitted to IRCC, therefore, if employers have concerns that they are not meeting conditions, they can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After
hiring a temporary worker) which is taken into consideration by the inspectors when assessing penalties for any violations of the conditions.

threads.answer:

### Good afternoon,
Question:
A client recently obtained a work permit when he arrived in Canada. He holds an Ethiopian passport and continues to do so. Yet he was recently approved forcitizenship and will be obtaining a passport. He will not be able to be a citizen of both Ethiopia and due to Ethiopian law, and thus will return his Ethiopian passport.
As his work permit was issued under his Ethiopian passport, will the work permit need to be corrected to reflect his new country of citizenship, or is no change to country of citizenship on the WP necessary?. Would this be done via a new application or an application to Amend a temporary residence document (IMM 1436). It in fact turns out that IRCC did not issue the work permit as requested (it restricted to one location, whereas we asked for no location restriction). Could we correct that error and at the same time via said correction change the country of citizenship? Thank you.
Response:
Changes made to personal information after the client entered Canada will not be amended on the work permit (including citizenship). This information needs to match that of the passport. If the information on the client's passport has changed, they should apply for a new temporary resident document (i.e. a new work permit). To do so, they can submit the following form: Application to Change Conditions or Extend Your Stay in Canada (IMM 5710).
Please note that the IMM 1436 is only for changing clerical errors. Corrections will not be made for major changes to the client's employment situation (such as a change of location) unless a clerical error was made. For more information, please refer to Guide 5218.
The “Employer Location" field of the work permit must match the original Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or the LMIA Exemption application submitted by the employer when the client first applied. If the “Employer Location" field does not match the LMIA/LMIA Exemption application submitted by the employer, than the client must apply for a new work permit (using the new passport).
We trust this information will be helpful to you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

À: Objet: RE: Online courses and PGWP-REP-2024-1340- Due 3-Sep-24
Hello!
The recently announced IRCC regulations indicate that international students with valid study permits may need to apply for a new study permit when changing their designated learning institution (DLl) in most situations. However, there are scenarios (below) that do not clearly align with the examples provided on the IRCC guidelines page. [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html)
1. Scenario 1: Prerequisite Courses at a Secondary Institution A student is currently enrolled in a degree program at a university (DLI) but requires prerequisite high school courses. These courses would be attended simultaneously at a secondary school while the student remains enrolled in their degree program at the university. Since the student is not changing their primary institution but is attending a single course at a secondary school, would they still be required to apply for a new study permit to take this course?
A: Secondary students whose permit only authorizes studies at the primary or secondary level must apply for a new study permit in order to pursue studies at the post-secondary level. This also applies to post-secondary study permit holders, whose permit names a DLl or limits their studies to the post-secondary level, who wish to attend a secondary school program/course, even though the student is not changing their primary institution. Therefore, individuals transitioning between post-secondary and secondary level need to get a new study permit by applying to extend their current one to attend a secondary school.
2. Scenario 2: Cross-Institutional Enrollment for a Single Course Some students encounter situations where a required course is unavailable at their current university (DLl). In such cases, they obtain a letter of permission from their primary institution to take the course at another DLi (university) for one term, with the intention of transferring the credit back to their primary DLl (the one listed on their study permit). In this scenario, since the student is not permanently changing their DLI but is only attending a single course at another institution temporarily, would they need to apply for a new study permit?
A: Since November 08, 2024, post-secondary study permit holders must be enrolled at the designated learning institution (DLI) named on their permit. If a study permit holder wishes to concurrently attend more than one DLI, they must apply for a study permit for each DLl at which they intend to study.
As these scenarios are not explicitly addressed in the current guidelines, clarification on these matters would greatly help us provide accurate advice to international students.
Thank you for your guidance.
Regards,
Citoyenneté Canada

# Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance.. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form.
Please see our response to your question:
Question 1: Does R222(1)(a.1) apply to students whose study permit does not name a designated learning institution on it?
Answer 1: If a student is no longer enrolled at the designated learning institution (DLl) named in their study permit and does not have the DLI's name on their study permit, then subparagraph IRPR 222(1)(a.1) would not be applicable to them.
Question 2: Does the 90-day window to restore status apply to students who lose their status under R222(1)(a.1)? For example, if a student withdraws and would like to wait to leave Canada while a refund of tuition for the future terms is processed (less than 90 days), must they take action to maintain their status in Canada (i.e. apply for visitor status before they withdraw), or, given the 90-day restoration period, can they remain in Canada without taking action for a maximum of 90 days?
Answer 2:
A study permit holder must meet their study permit conditions. In such cases where the student is withdrawn due to not meeting previous study permit conditions, the student is considered "no longer enrolled". If you do not abide to the conditions of your study permit you may need to change your status, or leave Canada. However, there are a few cases where a student may be able to take a leave of up to a maximum of 150 days from their program of studies and still be actively pursuing their studies.
For more information, please refer to the IRCC website
Question 3: If a student withdraws from their DLl, but applies and is accepted to a different program at the same DLI starting 150 days or less after withdrawing from the initial program, and the study permit's expiry date has not passed, can they continue studying with the same study permit, or, given R111(1)(a.1), must they apply for a new study permit?
Answer 3: Students may, in exceptional circumstances, take a leave from their studies. The student must resume classes within 150 days of the date on which they stopped studying. There are various examples of reasons listed on the IRCC website Study Permits: Assessing study permit conditions-Canada.ca such as a change in program of study within the same institution. As of November 8, 2024, IRCC compliance reports are mandatory where the DLI must select the appropriate student's academic status at the DLI. IRCC's website provides several enrollment status options such as leave of absence, deferred enrollment, academic suspension, no longer registered etc. We ask you that you carefully review each definition.
Academic suspension The student is suspended from your institution, due to poor academic performance or violation of the institution's policies. The student is allowed to return after the period of suspension.
Any leave from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 consecutive days from the date the leave started. If a student exceeds 150 days of leave from studies, they will need to change their status with IRCC or will be considered non- compliant with their study permit conditions.
No longer registered or enrolled Your institution sent the student a letter of admission, but they are no longer registered or enrolled because they have
- * been dismissed
* withdrawn voluntarily
- * transferred to another institution
Therefore, there is a difference between a student returning after a suspension and one no longer registered due to a withdrawal. If a student withdraws and is no longer enrolled at a DLl, they are no longer meeting the conditions of their study permit.
Question 4: If a student withdraws from their DLl, but applies and is accepted to resume the same program at the same DLl starting 150 days or less after withdrawing from the initial program, and the study permit's expiry date has not passed, can they continue studying with the same study permit, or, given R111(1)(a.1), must they apply for a new study permit?
Answer 4: See above
Thank you kindly,

For the purposes of the designation, flagpoling, is defined as:
when foreign nationals, who hold temporary resident status in Canada, leave Canada and after a visit to the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon, re-enter for the purpose of obtaining immigration services at a port of entry including work and study permits.
1. 1. An applicant is not required to disclose if they intend to, or have, flagpoled when completing and submitting an application with IRCC under Canada's permanent resident economic pathways.
2. 2. An applicant is not required to disclose they have flagpoled in the past. However, the IRPA obligates persons under examination to be truthful in answering questions and providing all relevant evidence that an officer reasonably requires. If a foreign national is asked whether they have been refused admission to Canada or any other country or territory, they should declare a previous denial of entry, even if it is a result of flagpoling. When it comes to duration of employment as per LMIA, officers may issue a work permit for lesser duration than the LMIA for
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) Section 52 requires a foreign national to hold a passport that is valid for the entire length of their stay. Processing officers issue a work permit for the duration of work indicated in the LMIA provided that the passport is valid for the entire period. Where the passport expires before the specified duration of work, the work permit must be issued for a shorter duration than identified in the LMIA. For example, if the LMiA work duration is 2 years but the foreign national's passport will expire in 1 year, the officer will issue a 1-year work permit.
When issuing a work permit based on an approved LMIA for foreign nationals who are working under paragraph R186(u) and applying to continue working with the same employer, the officer calculates the extension period from the expiry date of the previous work permit and not from the date of approval. This ensures that the duration of work as stated in the LMIA is respected. For example, if the employment duration in the LMIA is 12 months and the foreign worker had been on maintained status with authority to work without a permit for 3 months before a decision was made on the work permit application, the officer would issue a work permit that is valid for 9 months from the date of the decision.
For more information on Duration of employment as per the LMIA, please consult: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-) refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-

Questions
- * Partant du fait qu'il n’est pas inscrit dans l’établissement B et que rien ne lui est reconnu par cet établissement, a-t-il besoin d’une autre autorisation que son permis d’études existant?
■* Réponse : Aucun autre permis d’études ne sera nécessaire puisque l’étudiant n’est pas inscrit à l’établissement B et n’y est pas reconnu.
- * Est-il juste de dire que, autant lorsqu’il va sur le terrain que lorsqu’il fait des essais dans l’établissement B, l’étudiant
Ln est autorisé à mener ses essais grâce à son permis d’études, car ce sont des activités directement liées à sa formation doctorale créditée dans l’établissement A? o * Si non, quelle autorisation devrait-il obtenir pour mener les activités décrites qui sont partie intégrante de son doctorat? ■* Réponse : Selon les informations fournies, les activités décrites pourraient exiger un permis de travail COOP. L’établissement devra fournir une lettre à l’étudiant qui explique l’exigence de faire des activités de recherches soit en entreprise, sur le terrain ou dans tout autre établissement dans le cadre son
programme de doctorat et d’y décrire les spécificités.
Commentaire : Que ce soit pour aller faire des expériences sur le terrain ou dans l'établissement B en lien avec son doctorat, il ne s'agit pas d'activités jugées professionnelles. Je ne vois pas en vertu de quelle définition on pourrait considérer que c'est du travail puisqu'il ne s'agit ni d'une activité pour laquelle quelqu'un serait habituellement payé ni d'une activité qui représente une expérience de travail.
Méme si on convenait qu'il s'agit de travail, puisque ces activités ne sont pas obligatoires dans les programmes d’études et qu'elles sont planifiées à la pièce selon le projet de l'étudiant, cela ne répond pas aux critères d'admissibilité du permis de travail COOP et il est impossible pour l'établissement de faire une lettre précisant que c'est une exigence du programme.
Et quelles seraient les programmes qui lui permettrait de les obtenir? ■* Réponse : Un permis de travail COOP est nécessaire pour tout programme qui nécessite un stage ou une activité jugée professionnelle. o * Si oui, existe-t-il de règles publiées à cet effet ou une jurisprudence sur le sujet? ■*Réponse : De plus amples informations sont disponibles sur le site internet d'IRCC. o * Si oui, et considérant que son doctorat est d’une durée prévue de 4 ans, combien de temps l’étudiant pourrait-
il mener des essais dans l’établissement B sans contrevenir aux conditions de son permis d’études?
■* Réponse : Dans le cadre d’un stage coop, ou professionnel, l’activité ne doit pas excéder 50% de la durée du programme.
Questions dérivées
- * Si le codirecteur de l’étudiant n’était pas associé à l’établissement A, le raisonnement resterait-il le même?
* Réponse: Oui.

*** Question: I would like to confirm if Maternity leave would mean not having continuous work for the purpose of Express entry category draws.
For example: A person was working for an employer as from May 2022 to August 2023; left for 1 year Maternity leave, starting in September 2023 and returned to the same empioyer, same position, however with part-time hours, in October
2024. Category draws require a person to have a minimum of 6 months continuous full-time work experience in the selected occupation. This person has over 780 hours if we add from May to August 2023 and from October 2024 to present. However, not yet if we consider from October 2024. Please clarify whether or not Maternity leave is considered an imterruption in continuous employment for the purposes of the category draw. Answer: When the work experience is entered into the Express Entry Profile Builder, the two separate periods of work experience will not be considered as continuous work experience. While the applicant is continuously employed, maternity leave would be considered an interruption in their continuous work experience. For the purposes of this requirement the work hours are calculated only when the applicant performs the duties under their occupation. Long periods of leave do not count as hours of performing the duties. Question: Can we count full time equivalent work experience accumulated as student? If yes, if someone worked 20 hours per week and achieved 780 hours in about 8 months of work would that be enough to count as full-time equivalent? Answer: Requirements differ between Express Entry programs regarding the eligibility of work experience gained as a student:
Canadian Experience Class (CEC):
- * Work experience gained while a candidate was a full-time student (even if the candidate was on a co-op work term) doesn't count toward the minimum requirements for the CEC program.
Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP):
- * Experience gained while studying may count towards a candidate's minimum requirements if the work:
o * was paid by wages or commissions
o * was continuous (no gaps in employment), and
o * meets all the other reguirements of the Program
For work hours, 780 hours in 8 months at 20 hours per week is not enough to meet the 1,560-hour minimum required for full-time equivalency. The candidate can meet the 1,560-hour requirement in a few different ways:
- * full time at 1 job: up to 30 hours/week for 12 months = 1 year full time (1,560 hours)
- * equal amount in part-time work: for example, 15 hours/week for 24 months = 1 year full time (1,560 hours) o * The candidate can work as many part-time jobs as are needed to meet this requirement.
- * full time at more than 1 job: 30 hours/week for 12 months at more than 1 job = 1 year full time (1,560 hours)
